title: Consistent application of production techniques and nursery processes

lessons.title: Why consistency matters in the nursery
lessons.html:
The same good result every time

Customers such as garden centres and landscapers want every plant in an order to look the same: same size, same shape, same health. That only happens when every worker uses the same correct technique every day. If one worker plants liners deeper than another, or one block is watered differently, the plants grow unevenly and the order cannot be filled from one batch.

What consistency gives the nursery

  • Uniform crops that are ready at the same time and are easy to sell.
  • Fewer losses, because proven methods are used.
  • Predictable timing, so production plans can be trusted.
  • Lower costs, because there is less rework and waste.
  • A good reputation with customers who come back.

Standard operating procedures

Many nurseries write their methods down as standard operating procedures (SOPs) or work instructions. An SOP for sticking cuttings might state: length of cutting, how many leaves to remove, whether to dip in rooting hormone, depth of insertion, spacing in the tray, labelling and placing in the mist house. SOPs make sure that everyone, including new workers, uses the same method.

In this work-experience module you will apply the nursery's techniques consistently in the workplace, under the guidance of your mentor or manager. You should get to know the SOPs for your nursery and keep evidence of your work, such as task records, checklists and supervisor sign-offs, for your portfolio.

lessons.title: Applying standard techniques at each stage
lessons.html:
Doing each task the nursery way

Below are typical points that must be done the same way every time. Your nursery's own SOP always takes priority.

Propagation

  • Use clean trays and fresh or treated medium.
  • Take cuttings from labelled, healthy stock plants only.
  • Cut to the standard length and insert to the standard depth.
  • Sow seed at the depth and density on the plan.
  • Label every tray straight away.

Potting and transplanting

  • Use the correct medium and container size for the product.
  • Fill containers to the same level.
  • Plant at the same depth as the plug or liner, in the centre, upright.
  • Firm gently and water in promptly.

Growing on

  • Follow the irrigation and feeding programme for each block.
  • Pinch or prune at the stage stated in the programme.
  • Space plants at the set time to keep shape and light even.
  • Scout for pests and diseases on a fixed weekly schedule.

Spraying

Only trained, authorised workers apply agricultural remedies, registered under Act 36 of 1947. Mix and apply exactly as the label states, wear the protective equipment shown, observe any re-entry period on the label, and record every application. Never spray in wind or when people are nearby without protection.

Finishing and dispatch

  • Grade plants against the product standard.
  • Clean pots, remove weeds and dead leaves.
  • Attach the correct label or price tag.
  • Pack and load so plants are not crushed or broken.

lessons.title: Keeping standards up across the team
lessons.html:
Making consistency a habit

Train to the standard

Train every worker on the SOP for each task they do. Use the method: explain, demonstrate, let them try, correct, then check later. Keep a training record. Retrain when a method changes or when a worker's work drifts from the standard.

Show the standard

Keep examples or photos of a correctly stuck tray, a correctly potted plant and a top-grade finished plant where workers can see them. People copy what they see more easily than what they read.

Check regularly

  • Spot-check work several times a day, for example ten pots from each worker.
  • Use simple checklists for key steps: depth, label, firmness, upright.
  • Check irrigation coverage and the feeding unit daily.
  • Compare batches: if one batch is weaker than others, find out what was done differently.

Correct quickly and fairly

When work is below standard, stop the error from spreading, show the worker the correct method, and check again soon. Focus on the method, not on blaming the person. Praise workers who keep the standard.

Record and learn

Keep records of methods used, dates, sprays, feeds, losses and quality results. Over time these records show which methods give the best results and help managers improve SOPs. Suggest improvements to SOPs to your manager rather than changing methods on your own.

Evidence for your portfolio

For this work-experience module, collect evidence that you applied techniques consistently: signed task lists, quality checklists, batch records, training records and feedback from your supervisor.

Key points

  • Consistent methods give uniform crops, fewer losses and reliable timing.
  • Follow the nursery's SOPs for every stage of production.
  • Only trained workers spray, following the label and recording each application.
  • Train, show, check and correct to keep standards up.
  • Suggest SOP changes to the manager rather than changing methods alone.

quiz.question: Why do customers want consistent plants in an order?

options.text: They want every plant to look the same in size, shape and health
They prefer plants of mixed sizes
Consistency makes plants cheaper to water

quiz.question: What is a standard operating procedure (SOP)?

options.text: A written method that everyone follows for a task

quiz.question: How deep should a liner be planted when potting, according to the standard techniques?

options.text: Much deeper than in the tray
At the same depth as the plug or liner
At any depth the worker prefers

quiz.question: One batch is weaker than the others. What should you do?

options.text: Find out what was done differently

quiz.question: You think an SOP could be improved. What should you do?

options.text: Suggest the improvement to your manager
Change the method on your own
Tell only one worker to use your method
